title: Common Production Pitfalls
summary: Most Go production incidents come from a small set of recurring traps: **goroutine leaks**, **nil-pointer panics from typed-nil interfaces**, **unbounded resource use**, missing **context** deadlines, and unclosed resources. None are exotic — they're the predictable consequences of a few easy-to-make mistakes. Knowing the pattern, the symptom, and the fix turns 3am pages into code-review comments.

subtopics.title: Goroutine leaks
subtopics.explanation: A goroutine blocked forever — on a channel with no peer, or with no cancellation path — never returns and holds its stack and any references. Memory and goroutine count climb until OOM. Every goroutine needs a guaranteed exit: a closed channel, a context cancellation, or a bounded select.
subtopics.example: select { case <-ctx.Done(): return; case v := <-ch: use(v) }

subtopics.title: Missing context deadlines
subtopics.explanation: A request with no timeout can hang forever, holding a goroutine, a connection, and downstream resources. Propagate context.Context with deadlines through call chains and honor ctx.Done(); a slow dependency must not become an unbounded hang.

subtopics.title: The typed-nil interface trap
subtopics.explanation: An interface is nil only when both its type and value are nil. Returning a nil *T as an error interface makes the interface non-nil (it carries the type *T), so `if err != nil` is true even though the pointer is nil — leading to surprising behavior or panics. Return the interface's nil literal, not a nil concrete pointer.
subtopics.example: var e *MyErr = nil; var err error = e; err != nil // true!

subtopics.title: Data races
subtopics.explanation: Concurrent access to the same memory with at least one write, without synchronization, is a data race: undefined behavior, corrupted data, or crashes that appear only under load. Guard shared state with a mutex or channels, and run tests with -race.
subtopics.example: go test -race ./...  // detects races during tests

subtopics.title: Unclosed resources & deferred-close errors
subtopics.explanation: Leaking file handles, HTTP response bodies, or DB rows exhausts limits and stalls the process. Always defer Close, drain and close http.Response.Body, and for writers check the error returned by Close (a deferred Close that swallows its error can hide data loss).

subtopics.title: Unbounded concurrency & memory retention
subtopics.explanation: Spawning one goroutine per request with no limit lets a load spike exhaust memory; bound it with a worker pool or semaphore. Separately, re-slicing a small window of a huge slice keeps the whole backing array alive — copy the window out so the big array can be collected.
subtopics.example: sem := make(chan struct{}, 100) // cap concurrency at 100

foundations.overview: Go makes concurrency and resource handling easy, which is exactly why the same few mistakes recur in production. A forgotten cancellation path leaks goroutines; a returned nil concrete pointer becomes a non-nil error interface; a request without a deadline hangs forever; shared state without a lock races; an unclosed body exhausts connections. These pitfalls are predictable and preventable. This lesson catalogs the highest-frequency Go production traps with their symptom, root cause, and idiomatic fix.
foundations.formalDefinition: Common Go production pitfalls are recurring failure modes — goroutine leaks, typed-nil interface confusion, missing context propagation, data races, and resource leaks — that arise from misusing Go's concurrency, interface, and resource-management primitives, and that surface as memory growth, hangs, panics, or corruption under production load.
foundations.whyItMatters: These bugs rarely fail in tests and instead manifest under real load — the worst time to discover them. Recognizing the patterns in code review prevents outages, and explaining them clearly is a hallmark of a senior Go engineer in interviews and on call.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of each goroutine, connection, and lock as a borrowed resource with a contract: you must give it back. A leak is a contract you never honored. The fixes are all variations of 'always provide an exit': cancellation for goroutines, deadlines for requests, defer-close for handles, and synchronization for shared memory.
foundations.runtimePerspective: The runtime tracks every goroutine; leaked ones show up in runtime.NumGoroutine() and the goroutine pprof profile, each holding a ≥2KB stack and whatever it references. An interface value is a (type, value) pair, so a non-nil type with a nil value is a non-nil interface. The race detector instruments memory accesses to flag unsynchronized read/write pairs. context cancellation closes a channel that select statements watch.
foundations.realWorldUsage: On-call engineers diagnose climbing NumGoroutine() as a leak, grep for returns of concrete error pointers, audit handlers for missing context timeouts and unclosed response bodies, and gate merges on go test -race and govulncheck.
foundations.businessImpact: A single goroutine leak or unbounded handler can OOM a fleet and cause a customer-facing outage; preventing these in review is dramatically cheaper than an incident, both in revenue and in engineer time.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Internalizing these patterns improves every code review and design: APIs accept context, goroutines get owners and exits, shared state gets synchronized, and resources get deferred closes — raising the whole team's reliability bar.
foundations.performanceImpact: Leaks and unbounded concurrency degrade gradually then collapse (OOM/connection exhaustion). The race detector adds overhead (so it runs in CI, not prod), but the bugs it catches cause unpredictable, hard-to-reproduce slowdowns and corruption.
commonUseCases: Auditing goroutines for a guaranteed exit path (cancellation/closed channel)
Propagating context with deadlines through request handling
Returning the nil error interface (not a nil concrete pointer)
Bounding concurrency with worker pools or semaphores and closing all resources

commonMisconceptions.myth: If a function returns a nil pointer as error, `err != nil` is false.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The interface carries the concrete type, so it's non-nil even with a nil value. Return `nil` (the interface) explicitly, or check the concrete type — don't assign a nil typed pointer into an error.

commonMisconceptions.myth: time.Sleep is a fine way to wait for goroutines.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's a race waiting to happen and a leak risk. Use sync.WaitGroup, channels, or context — never timing guesses.

commonMisconceptions.myth: One goroutine per request is always fine.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Unbounded, a load spike spawns unbounded goroutines and OOMs. Bound concurrency with a pool or semaphore and always set deadlines.

config.intro: How an on-call engineer tracks down a leak:

steps.name: Spot the symptom
steps.detail: Memory climbs steadily and runtime.NumGoroutine() rises monotonically without leveling off.

steps.name: Pull a goroutine profile
steps.detail: Fetch /debug/pprof/goroutine and look for many goroutines stuck on the same channel or select line.

steps.name: Find the missing exit
steps.detail: The stuck goroutines have no cancellation path — typically a send/receive with no peer, or no ctx.Done() case.

steps.name: Add a guaranteed exit
steps.detail: Introduce context cancellation, close the channel, or add a ctx.Done() case to the select.

steps.name: Verify
steps.detail: After the fix, NumGoroutine() stabilizes; a leak test asserts it returns to baseline.

interactiveExamples.title: The typed-nil interface gotcha
interactiveExamples.explanation: doWork returns a *MyError that is nil, but assigned into the error interface it becomes non-nil because the interface carries the type. The caller's `err != nil` is true even though nothing went wrong. The fix is to return the literal nil for the success path.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: stop the goroutine leak
interactiveExamples.explanation: search launches a goroutine that sends on an unbuffered channel, but main returns after the first result, leaving the others blocked forever — a leak. Add cancellation (context or a buffered channel) so every goroutine can exit. Fix the code.

code.expectedOutput:
result for a
(result order may vary)

checkpoints.prompt: What does this print, and why is it surprising?
checkpoints.explanation: f returns a nil *E assigned into the error interface. An interface is nil only when BOTH its type and value are nil; here the type is *E, so the interface is non-nil and f() == nil is false. Return literal nil on the success path to avoid this trap.

checkpoints.prompt: This handler compiles and usually works, but under load the service exhausts file descriptors. What's the bug?
options: resp.Body is never closed, leaking the connection/file descriptor on every request
io.ReadAll cannot read an HTTP body
w.Write must be called before reading the body
checkpoints.explanation: Every response body must be closed (defer resp.Body.Close()) to release the connection back to the pool / free the descriptor. Without it, each request leaks a connection until the process hits its fd limit. Also use a client with a timeout instead of http.Get's default.

checkpoints.prompt: A request handler calls a slow downstream service. What is the idiomatic way to ensure it can't hang forever?
options: Wrap the call in a goroutine and ignore it after a while
Use time.Sleep to limit how long you wait
Pass a context with a deadline (context.WithTimeout) and have the call honor ctx.Done()
Retry in an infinite loop until it responds
checkpoints.explanation: Propagate a context.Context with a deadline and ensure the downstream call (and any select) honors ctx.Done(). This bounds the wait, frees the goroutine and connection on timeout, and is the standard Go cancellation mechanism. Sleeps and abandoned goroutines leak resources.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the line so concurrent increments of counter are safe.
checkpoints.codeBefore:
var mu sync.Mutex
var counter int
func inc() {
    mu.Lock()
checkpoints.explanation: After Lock you must release the mutex; defer mu.Unlock() guarantees it runs even if the body panics. Without synchronization, concurrent counter++ is a data race (read-modify-write on shared memory) that -race would flag.

codeLab.title: Bound concurrency with a semaphore and honor context
codeLab.instructions: Implement `FetchAll(ctx, ids, max, fetch)` that calls `fetch(ctx, id)` for every id, running at most `max` concurrently, and returns the results in input order. If ctx is cancelled, stop launching new work. The harness checks ordering, the concurrency cap, and cancellation.
hints: A buffered channel of capacity max acts as a counting semaphore: send to acquire a slot, receive to release.
Write each result into out[idx]; distinct indices mean no data race, so no mutex is needed for the results.
Select on ctx.Done() before acquiring a slot so cancellation stops launching new goroutines; wg.Wait() before returning.

debuggingLab.title: WaitGroup misuse plus a closure capture race
debuggingLab.symptom: On Go 1.21 and earlier, this code prints duplicates/wrong values and occasionally the program exits before all work prints; go test -race flags a data race.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two classic bugs. First, wg.Add(1) is called inside the goroutine, so wg.Wait() can observe a zero counter before any goroutine is scheduled and return immediately. Second, on Go 1.21- the loop variable `it` is shared across iterations, so all goroutines may print the last value — and the concurrent read of `it` while the loop reassigns it is a data race. (Go 1.22 fixed the loop-variable sharing, but the Add-placement bug remains.)
commonMistakes: Calling wg.Add inside the goroutine instead of before `go`.
Capturing the loop variable in a closure instead of passing it as an argument.
Relying on Go 1.22 loop semantics for code that must also work on older versions.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Call Add before launching, and pass the loop value as an argument so each goroutine has its own copy.

solution.expectedOutput: (each item printed exactly once; order may vary; -race clean)

theory.question: What is a goroutine leak, how do you detect it, and how do you prevent it?
theory.directAnswer: A goroutine leak is a goroutine that blocks forever and never returns — typically on a channel send/receive with no peer, or with no cancellation path — so it holds its stack and references indefinitely. You detect it by watching runtime.NumGoroutine() climb monotonically and by pulling a goroutine pprof profile to see where they're stuck. You prevent it by giving every goroutine a guaranteed exit: context cancellation, a closed channel, a buffered channel so sends can't block, or a select with a ctx.Done() case.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Unbounded accumulation of goroutines that can never make progress.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A goroutine blocked on a channel or syscall with no counterpart parks forever.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The runtime keeps the parked goroutine and its stack alive; the count and memory grow until OOM.

theory.whyImportant: Goroutine leaks are one of the most common Go production incidents and a frequent interview probe.
theory.realWorldExample: A request spawns a goroutine that sends on an unbuffered channel, but the reader returns early on error, leaving the sender blocked forever.

followUps.question: How do you write a test that catches a leak?
followUps.answer: Record runtime.NumGoroutine() before, run the code, then assert it returns to baseline after a short settle — or use a library like goleak in TestMain.

followUps.question: Why does a buffered channel sometimes fix a leak?
followUps.answer: If the buffer is large enough for all sends, senders never block waiting for a receiver, so they can complete and exit even if no one reads.

theory.question: Explain the typed-nil interface pitfall. Why can a function that returns a nil pointer still produce a non-nil error?
theory.directAnswer: An interface value holds two things: a concrete type and a value. It is nil only when both are nil. If you assign a nil concrete pointer (e.g. var p *MyError = nil) into an error interface, the interface stores the type *MyError with a nil value, so the interface itself is non-nil — and `err != nil` is true. The fix is to return the literal nil for the success path, never a nil concrete pointer typed as the interface.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The mismatch between a nil concrete pointer and a nil interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Interfaces are (type, value) pairs; a non-nil type makes the interface non-nil regardless of the value.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Returning a typed nil pointer boxes it into the interface with its type, so nil checks on the interface fail.

theory.whyImportant: It causes baffling bugs where error handling fires on success, and it's a favorite interview gotcha.
theory.realWorldExample: A function declared to return error returns a *CustomErr that's nil on success; callers then wrongly treat success as failure.

followUps.question: How do you avoid it structurally?
followUps.answer: Don't declare a concrete error pointer variable and return it; return nil directly on success, or only construct and return the error type on the failure path.

followUps.question: Does this apply to interfaces beyond error?
followUps.answer: Yes — any interface. A nil *T assigned to any interface variable yields a non-nil interface carrying type *T.

scenario.question: A Go API service's memory and goroutine count climb steadily over hours until it OOMs and restarts, repeating in a cycle. Walk through diagnosing and fixing it.
scenario.directAnswer: The pattern — monotonic memory and NumGoroutine() growth — is a goroutine leak. Confirm by scraping runtime.NumGoroutine() as a metric and pulling /debug/pprof/goroutine, which will show many goroutines stuck on the same channel or select line. The root cause is almost always a goroutine started per request with no exit path: a send to a channel whose reader returned early, or a downstream call with no context deadline. Fix it by propagating a context with a timeout, adding a ctx.Done() case to the select, closing channels, or buffering so sends can't block — and add a leak test plus a NumGoroutine alert to prevent regression.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A slow-burn resource exhaustion from leaked goroutines.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Per-request goroutines without a guaranteed exit accumulate as traffic flows.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Each leaked goroutine holds a stack and references; the heap and goroutine count grow until OOM.

scenario.whyImportant: This exact incident shape is extremely common in Go services and a staple of senior on-call interviews.
scenario.realWorldExample: A timeout-less http.Get inside a per-request goroutine leaked one goroutine and one connection per slow upstream call.

followUps.question: What metric alert would catch this earlier?
followUps.answer: Alert on monotonically increasing runtime.NumGoroutine() (or a goroutines-per-request ratio) rather than waiting for the OOM.

followUps.question: How do context deadlines help?
followUps.answer: They guarantee the goroutine and its downstream call unblock at the deadline, providing the exit path that prevents the leak.

coding.question: Implement `func DoWithTimeout(ctx context.Context, work func() (int, error)) (int, error)` that runs work in a goroutine but returns ctx.Err() if the context is cancelled first — without leaking the goroutine.
coding.thoughtProcess: I run work in a goroutine that sends its result on a channel, then select on that channel versus ctx.Done(). The trap is leaking the goroutine if ctx fires first and work is still running. To avoid the leak, the result channel must be buffered (capacity 1) so the goroutine's send always succeeds and it can exit even when no one is selecting on it anymore.
coding.lineByLine: done is buffered with capacity 1 — this is the key to not leaking. The goroutine runs work and sends the result; because the channel has a slot, the send succeeds even if the main path already returned via ctx.Done(), so the goroutine exits instead of blocking forever. The select races the work's completion against context cancellation: if ctx fires first we return ctx.Err(); otherwise we return the work's result. An unbuffered channel here would leak the goroutine whenever the timeout wins.
coding.timeComplexity: O(1) coordination overhead; wall-clock is min(work duration, timeout).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(1) — one buffered slot and one goroutine.

followUps.question: Why must the channel be buffered?
followUps.answer: If ctx.Done() wins the select, no one ever receives from an unbuffered channel, so the goroutine's send blocks forever — a leak. A buffer of 1 lets it send and exit.

followUps.question: Can work itself be cancelled?
followUps.answer: Only if it accepts and honors the context. This pattern unblocks the caller, but truly stopping work requires work to check ctx.Done() internally.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Make every goroutine have an owner responsible for stopping it, and thread context.Context (with deadlines) through all request paths. Bound concurrency at the edges with worker pools or semaphores so load spikes can't spawn unbounded goroutines. Close every resource you open with defer.
productionDeepDive.performance: Leaks and unbounded concurrency degrade gradually then collapse; pre-size buffers, reuse with sync.Pool on hot paths, and copy small windows out of large slices so big backing arrays can be collected. Profile with pprof (heap, goroutine, alloc) under realistic load.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Run go test -race in CI to catch data races before they ship. Prefer channels/context to shared mutable state; when you must share, guard with sync.Mutex (defer Unlock) and keep critical sections small. Pass loop values as arguments to goroutines.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Every goroutine needs a guaranteed exit (cancellation, closed channel, or bounded select). Wrap long-lived worker loops with recover so a single panic doesn't crash the process, and always set deadlines on external calls so a slow dependency can't hang you.
productionDeepDive.observability: Export runtime.NumGoroutine() and heap metrics and alert on monotonic growth. Expose /debug/pprof for live goroutine and heap profiles. Wrap errors with %w and log with context so failures are traceable to a request and commit.
productionDeepDive.security: Synchronize shared state so races can't corrupt security-relevant decisions, bound concurrency to resist resource-exhaustion DoS, set timeouts so slowloris-style clients can't tie up goroutines, and never leak other requests' data through reused buffers.

caseStudies.problem: Per-request goroutines with timeout-less downstream calls leaked goroutines and connections, causing periodic OOM restarts.
caseStudies.solution: Propagate context deadlines, buffer result channels, and add NumGoroutine alerting plus goleak-based leak tests.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: A little extra plumbing (context everywhere) for durable stability.
caseStudies.lessons: Most Go OOMs trace back to a missing exit path; deadlines and bounded channels are the cure.

caseStudies.company: Teams adopting the race detector in CI
caseStudies.problem: Intermittent data corruption under load from unsynchronized shared maps.
caseStudies.solution: Gate merges on go test -race, replace shared maps with sync.Mutex-guarded access or sync.Map, and pass loop values as arguments.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Race-detected test runs are slower and use more memory, so they run in CI rather than every local run.
caseStudies.lessons: Races that never fail in dev fail catastrophically in production; -race in CI is cheap insurance.

keyTakeaways: Most Go production incidents are a handful of recurring traps: goroutine leaks, typed-nil interfaces, missing context deadlines, data races, and unclosed resources.
Give every goroutine a guaranteed exit (context cancellation, closed/buffered channel, or a ctx.Done() select) and bound concurrency with pools or semaphores.
An interface is nil only when its type AND value are nil — return literal nil on success, never a nil concrete pointer; and always defer Close on resources.
Catch these before production: run go test -race, set deadlines on external calls, watch runtime.NumGoroutine() with pprof, and review for missing exits in code review.
